title: The silver cup (Genesis 44)
hookLine: Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers himself in Benjamin's place

cards: The grain runs out. Jacob refuses, again and again, to let Benjamin go. Finally Judah steps up: put him in my care, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever.
In Egypt the governor throws them a feast, seats them in birth order, which unnerves them, and gives Benjamin five times as much. They leave at dawn, sacks full, Simeon free, relieved.
Then the governor's steward catches up: one of you has stolen my master's silver cup. So sure it's a mistake, they say, whoever has it shall die. The steward searches, oldest to youngest.

teach.h: THE OFFER: KEEP THE THIEF, GO HOME.
teach.b: Joseph planted the cup. It's his last test. The brothers tear their clothes and all go back.
Then the governor offers them exactly what they once chose: the thief stays as my slave; the rest of you go home in peace. The old situation, set up again. A favored son of Rachel.
A chance to be rid of him, and this time they could even say it wasn't their fault. And Judah steps forward.
This is the brother who said, years ago at the pit, let's sell him. Genesis has followed him since: he wronged his daughter-in-law Tamar, and ended up admitting she was more righteous than he.

Now he makes a long, careful plea. He tells of their old father, who lost one son of the wife he loved, and whose life is bound up in the boy's life. If the boy doesn't come home, the old man will die.
Then, in the King James Bible: "Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren."
"For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me?"

teach.h: TAKE ME INSTEAD OF THE LAD.
HOW SHALL I GO UP TO MY FATHER, AND THE LAD BE NOT WITH ME?
teach.b: The man who sold one brother into slavery offers himself as a slave to save the other. That is the change the test was looking for.
Some Christian readers see in Judah a picture of the one who gives himself in another's place, and note that Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family line through Judah.

how: Some Christians read Judah's offer as a picture of substitution, someone giving himself in another's place, and preachers set it beside Jesus's death; Matthew 1 traces Jesus's line through Judah.

games.q: you're Judah. the governor says: the boy with the cup stays as my slave; the rest of you, go home in peace. your father will die if the boy doesn't come back. what do you do?
o: go home and tell your father it couldn't be helped.
offer to stay as a slave instead of the boy.
try to fight your way out.
games.why: "let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord." the brother who sold Joseph offers himself to save Benjamin.

practice: Someone near you may be carrying a load they can't really carry: a coworker, a sibling, a neighbor.
Picture taking one piece of it on, a shift, a chore, a hard conversation so they don't have to, and notice what it would cost, and what it would give. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Judah. The brother who once sold Joseph, now offering himself as a slave in Benjamin's place: the test that showed he had changed.

orig.note: Hebrew: Judah. Genesis links his name to praise, from his mother Leah's words at his birth.

carryVoice: Your line: take me instead. Judah offered to stay so Benjamin could go home. That's day three hundred seventy-two.
